Neural Network Field Guide

PDF, for print (opens in a new tab)PNG, light (opens in a new tab)PNG, dark (opens in a new tab)

42 architectures and training schemes, from the perceptron (1958) to diffusion LLMs (2025).

Each diagram draws a network in miniature, input at the bottom and output at the top; one that settles as a whole is a ring, and a graph network is its graph. Most circles are neurons; in sequence models a column is a token, a circle its vector at one layer. A square is larger: an image patch, a matrix-valued state, a whole network, or an environment. Color and mark both show a cell’s role, so diagrams read without color. Faded parts play little role in the step shown. Parts repeated over positions, windows, copies, or passes share weights; layers, experts, encoders, and decoders drawn alike do not. Sections group by trait: wiring, dynamics, training, cost, or purpose. Years and methods follow landmark papers, not always the first. Select a diagram for its explanation, key, and papers.

What is a neural network?

A network of simple units

A neural network is built from simple . Most take in numbers, multiply each by a , add them up, and pass the sum through a simple . Units are arranged in , and each layer's outputs feed the next, so simple steps stack into a complicated function of the input. A few panels use units that work differently: some measure a distance to a stored point (RBF), and some apply a learned curve to each input (KAN).

An example: the MLP

In this network, three numbers pass up through two of four units to two outputs, along 36 , one weight each. Move the inputs: each unit adds up what arrives, each value scaled by its line's weight, and squashes the sum to between 0 and 1. Thicker lines carry larger weights, and gray ones subtract; brighter units are more active. Training changes only the weights; the wiring stays as drawn. Randomize weights draws a fresh random set, like a network before training. Real networks also learn a , a number added to each unit's sum; the drawings and this demo leave it out.

The MLP uses only four of the symbols below, each first in its list: the input unit, hidden unit, output unit and connection. The rest appear in other panels, for memory, , and more; each panel's key lists the ones it uses.

Every mark and link

Each color and outer mark names a role, and a cell's shape or a small mark inside it names the kind.

Input

Yellow, with a stem below: data entering the network.

  • Input unit. One number, or one token's vector, fed in.
  • Image patch. A square tile of an image, fed in as one vector.
  • Noisy input. Data with noise added, which the network learns to clean up.
  • Random noise. Random numbers drawn fresh each time, which a generator turns into data.
  • Visible unit (in and out). Set by the data, then updated by the network: in Hopfield and Boltzmann machines the same units are both input and output.
  • Masked token. A token hidden from the network, which it must guess. Hollow, since its value is missing.

Hidden

Green and unmarked: work that stays inside.

  • Hidden unit. Adds up what arrives along its lines and applies a nonlinearity.
  • Probabilistic hidden. Turns on at random, with odds set by its inputs; in the VAE, a code sampled from a learned distribution.
  • Capsule (vector output). Outputs a vector: its length says whether a part is present, its direction how it is posed.
  • Router. Scores the experts and sends each token to the best few.

State

Blue, with a ring: something kept from one step to the next.

  • Recurrent unit. Holds a vector it updates at each step from the new input and its last value.
  • Memory cell. A store kept apart from the working state, written and read by the network: the LSTM's cell, the NTM's memory, Modern Hopfield's stored patterns.
  • Matrix-valued state. A state that is a whole matrix rather than a vector, updated at each step.

Mixing

Pink, with a tick each side: a unit that combines values from many positions.

  • Attention. Weighs every other position by how well it matches, then mixes their values in those proportions. In a Transformer it usually stands for a whole block, attention and the feed-forward layer after it (the decoder's block spans its two attention rows).
  • Convolution or pooling. Applies one small filter at every window of its input, or pools a window into one value.

Output

Red, with a stem above: data leaving the network.

  • Output unit. A result: a prediction, a class score, the next token.
  • Reconstruction of input. The network's attempt to rebuild its own input.
  • Velocity. Which way, and how fast, to move a noisy sample toward real data.

Whole systems

Gray: a whole network as one box.

  • A whole network. Any architecture: an expert, a generator, a denoiser. Panels that show a way of training draw networks this way, since any can fill the role.
  • Environment. The world an agent acts in, outside the network: it takes an action and returns the next state and a reward.

Links

Every line is drawn at one weight; only the dash, the arrowhead or the path differs.

  • Connection. One weight between single units: the value below is scaled by it on the way up. Between whole vectors it is a matrix of weights.
  • Skip connection. Carries a layer's input around it, to be added to its output or joined to a later layer.
  • Data passed on or fed back. Data carried one way: a state to the next step, a message to a neighbor, or, bent around the side, an output fed back in to run the network again.
  • Gate, acting at the dot. A learned signal that sets how much passes along the arrow it meets, at the dot.
  • Similarity score. A weight computed from the input by how well two things match, as in every attention read (what passes still goes through learned weights shared by every line), or the match score itself, as in a similarity.
  • Learnable function. A small learned function in place of a single weight.

Learning means adjusting weights

A network starts with random weights. Training shows it examples, scores how wrong its output is with a (the objective), and nudges every weight to make that score better; works out which way each weight should move. Over many examples, the weights come to encode the task. Most panels here learn this way; a few use local rules instead, such as Hopfield's rule and the Kohonen map's rule.

The test is new data

Fitting the training examples isn't the goal; doing well on examples the network hasn't seen is. A network with enough weights can memorize its training set, quirks and errors included, and then fail on anything new. That is , so a network is judged on held-out examples, kept out of training.

Two things keep it general. limits how freely it fits: weight decay keeps weights small, dropout switches off random units in training, and data augmentation shows each example in many variations. And every architecture assumes something about its data before seeing any, its : a , that a pattern means the same anywhere in an image; a network, that order matters; a network, that the graph's do. A good assumption saves data. Attention builds in fewer assumptions about images, which is why the original ViT needed more images than a CNN to match it.

Architectures differ in wiring

Those assumptions live mostly in the wiring: what sets most designs apart is which units connect. connect every unit to every unit in the next layer; convolutions connect small and reuse the same weights across them; recurrent networks carry a from one step to the next; attention lets each weigh every other by its content.

Inside a Transformer block

A Transformer stacks one kind of , run the same way at every position. Here one position goes through it: attention reads from it and the positions before it (in an , from all of them); then a small MLP, the , works on that position alone, widening its (to four units here, often four times its size) and narrowing it back. Around each step a adds the step's input to its output, and the sum is (most recent models normalize before each step instead). The panels usually draw all of this as one pink attention cell (the Transformer's spreads its block over two attention rows), and leave out position: the original Transformer adds it to each once, before the first block, while most recent models build it into attention in every block (rotary , RoPE).

Training schemes differ in the goal

The same network can be trained toward different goals: to predict labels, the next word, or a hidden one, or to new data, as GANs and do. Panels that show a way of training draw the networks inside as gray boxes, since any network can fill them.

Reading a diagram

Data flows from the inputs at the bottom to the outputs at the top. Each circle is a unit (in sequence models, a whole token's vector), each line a connection (one weight in the MLP), and a cell's color and mark show its role, as the key explains. The diagrams show how parts connect, not complete implementations: normalization, most residual paths and positional information are left out. Select any diagram for its explanation, how it is trained, and where it came from. Step through lights each unit once everything it reads has lit, so stacked layers move along a sequence as a diagonal wave.

Basics

Activation

A unit's output value for a given input: its weighted sum after the . The activations of a together are its representation of the input.

Used in: Every network here.

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab)

Activation function

The function a unit applies to its weighted sum, such as (keep positive values, zero out the rest) or a sigmoid (squash any number into 0 to 1). Without one, a stack of weighted sums with nothing nonlinear between them would collapse into a single , however deep. KAN learns its functions instead of fixing them. The perceptron's is a hard threshold: on above it, off below.

Used in: Nearly every network here; KAN learns its functions instead of fixing them.

Source: Nair & Hinton 2010 (opens in a new tab); Glorot, Bordes & Bengio 2011 (opens in a new tab)

Bias

A number a unit adds to its weighted sum, learned like a . It sets how easily the unit responds, so it can fire even when its inputs are all zero.

Used in: Nearly every network here.

Source:

Class

One of the categories a classifier sorts inputs into, such as cat or dog, or the digits 0 to 9. A classifier usually gives one output per class, turned into by a .

Used in: , , , , , , ,

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab)

Deep learning

Machine learning with networks of many , each finding built from those of the layer below. It took off in the late 2000s and early 2010s, once more data, faster hardware, and better training methods made deep networks practical; most networks here from the DBN on are deep.

Used in: Nearly every network here; the perceptron, the Hopfield network, and the Kohonen map are shallow.

Source: LeCun, Bengio & Hinton 2015 (opens in a new tab)

Dense and sparse

A dense (fully connected) links every unit to every unit of the layer before.

Sparse means few: a sparse has only a few units active at once, as in a sparse autoencoder, and a sparse runs only a few experts per .

Used in: , , , ,

Source: ;

Embedding

A learned that stands for an item, such as a , an image, or a sentence.

Training can place items near each other when they are alike in the way its task needs, so distance in the space comes to mean something. (2013) made learned word vectors the standard starting point for language.

Used in: , , , , , ,

Source: Bengio et al. 2003 (opens in a new tab); Mikolov et al. 2013 (opens in a new tab)

Feature

A property of the input that a unit responds to, such as an edge, a texture, or a word's tense. A 's output, one feature measured at every position, is a feature map.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab)

Hidden layer

A between the input and the output, whose values no one sets or reads directly.

Hidden layers, with a nonlinear , let a network build its own , which is what lets it learn more than a straight-line boundary.

Used in: , , , , , ,

Source:

Inductive bias

What a model assumes about its data before seeing any, built into its design. A assumes that nearby pixels matter most and that a pattern means the same wherever it appears; a network, that order matters; a network, that the graph's say what is related. An assumption that fits the data saves data, and one that doesn't holds the model back. builds in fewer assumptions about images (neither that nearby pixels matter most nor that a pattern means the same anywhere), which is why the original ViT needed more training images than a CNN to match it, until better training recipes narrowed the gap, and why it keeps improving when images are plentiful.

Discussed in: ,

Source: Battaglia et al. 2018 (opens in a new tab);

Input and output

The input is the data a network is given, such as an image's pixels or a sentence's ; the output is what it produces, such as a label, the , or an image. The guide marks them with stems: below an input, above an output.

Used in: Every network here.

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab)

Layer

A stage of computation that turns one representation into the next, usually a row of units working side by side.

A network's depth is its number of layers. In the guide's drawings a row is one stage of the computation, often one layer, but a row can also stand for a whole (a Transformer's and the after it), so counting rows doesn't give a model's depth.

Used in: Every network here.

Source:

Link

A line between two cells in the guide's diagrams. Its style says what it carries: a plain line a learned , dashed a weight set by similarity, dotted a , an arrow data passed on, a wavy line a learned function. The key lists them.

Used in: Every network here.

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab)

Parameters

A network's learned numbers: its and . A can have many parameters but use only a few experts per , so its active parameters, the ones each token runs through, are far fewer.

Used in: Every network here.

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab);

Patch

One of the small squares an image is cut into, flattened into a and treated as a . ViT-B/16 reads a 224-by-224 image as 196 patches of 16 by 16 pixels; other patch sizes and resolutions give other counts.

Used in: ,

Source:

Probability distribution

How likely each possible outcome is, adding up to 1 over all of them: each , , or a network might choose, or, for numbers that vary smoothly, how densely they fall in each range (a 's bell curve). turns scores into one; learn one over their data and from it.

Used in: , , , , , ,

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab)

ReLU

Rectified linear unit: the that passes a positive sum unchanged and turns a negative one to zero.

Cheap, and easy to train through many , it became the default in in the early 2010s.

Used in: , , ,

Source: Nair & Hinton 2010 (opens in a new tab); Glorot, Bordes & Bengio 2011 (opens in a new tab)

Softmax

A function that turns a list of scores into that are positive and add up to 1, giving the largest scores most of the weight.

uses it to weigh positions, a to turn scores into the 's .

Used in: , , , , , , , , , ,

Source: Bridle 1989 (opens in a new tab)

Target

The output training wants for an input: the right label, the actual , or the direction a flow should move. The measures how far the output is from it.

Used in: Nearly every network here; not the Hopfield network, the Kohonen map, the Boltzmann machine or RBM, or a GAN's generator, which learn without a set answer for each input.

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab)

Token

One item of a sequence as a model reads it: a word or part of a word, an image , a sound sample. Each becomes a before the network sees it.

Used in: , , , , , , , , ,

Source: Sennrich, Haddow & Birch 2016 (opens in a new tab)

Unit

The basic element of a network, also called a neuron: it multiplies each input by a , adds them up with a , and passes the sum through an . The guide draws one as a circle.

Used in: Every network here.

Source: McCulloch & Pitts 1943 (opens in a new tab);

Vector

An ordered list of numbers, such as a unit's or a 's : a point, or a direction, in a space with one axis per number.

Most of what flows through a network is vectors.

Used in: Every network here.

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab)

Weight

A number on a connection that scales whatever passes along it. Training adjusts the weights; they are what a network learns. Most lines in the guide stand for one.

Used in: Every network here.

Source:

XOR

Exclusive or: true when exactly one of two inputs is on.

Its true and false cases can't be split by one straight line, so a perceptron can't learn it, while a network with a can; Minsky and Papert's 1969 analysis of such limits is often blamed for slowing the field for years.

Used in: ,

Source: Minsky & Papert 1969 (opens in a new tab);

Operations

Associative memory

A memory recalled by content rather than address: given part of a stored pattern, or a copy, it returns the whole. Its capacity is how many patterns it can store before recall breaks down.

Used in: ,

Source: ;

Attention

A way for each position in a sequence to gather what it needs from the others, taking more from the positions that match it best: its against their keys.

The are set by the input itself, unlike a 's learned weights, which is why the guide draws them dashed. Self-attention reads the same sequence; cross-attention reads another, such as the source sentence in . A layer usually runs several at once, each a (multi-head attention).

Used in: , , , , , , , , , ,

Source: ;

Bidirectional

Reading a sequence both ways, so each position sees what comes after it as well as before.

An may read its input both ways, as BERT's does, or in one direction only, as the first seq2seq encoders did. A model writing one at a time can't see tokens it hasn't written yet, but it can still read an input it is given, such as the sentence to , both ways. Processing every position at once isn't the same thing: GPT trains on all positions , yet each reads only to its left.

Used in: , , , , , ,

Source: ;

Block

A small group of repeated to build a , such as a Transformer's and with their . Stacking the same block many times is how most deep networks are made; the primer opens one.

Used in: , , , , , , , ,

Source: ;

Bottleneck

The narrowest of a network that squeezes its input and widens it again, which forces it to keep only what matters most for its task, such as rebuilding the input.

In an autoencoder the bottleneck is the ; in U-Net it is the coarsest scale, with carrying the fine detail around it.

Used in: , ,

Source: ;

Capsule

A group of units whose output is a : its length says how likely an entity is present, and its direction describes it, such as its pose. Capsules pass their outputs on by by agreement.

Used in:

Source:

Causal mask

In a model that a sequence, each position may read only itself and the ones before it, never later ones.

Its is the next position, so in training it cannot see what it is learning to predict. The guide draws it as lines that reach back or straight up, never forward. WaveNet gets the same effect from causal , which only look back.

Used in: , , ,

Source:

Channel

One of the stacked maps at each position of a , such as red, green, and blue in an image, or one 's output deeper in. A filter reads every channel in its , and each filter makes one new channel.

Used in: , , , ,

Source:

Clamping

Holding some units fixed at given values, such as the visible units at a training example, while the rest of the network settles or is around them.

Used in: , ,

Source:

Code

The representation an makes of its input, from which a rebuilds it: usually smaller than the input, or, in a autoencoder, with only a few units active at once.

Used in: , , ,

Source: ; Hinton & Salakhutdinov 2006 (opens in a new tab)

Convolution

Applying one small set of , a , at every position of the input, so a pattern is detected wherever it appears.

Each output reads only a few neighbors, and every position shares the same weights, so the weights stay few. Stacked see wider and wider regions: in an image, early filters find edges and later ones shapes. WaveNet's convolutions skip inputs, so a few layers reach far back.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: ;

Cosine similarity

How closely two point the same way, from 1 (same direction) through 0 (perpendicular) to −1 (opposite), whatever their lengths: a common score for comparing .

Whether perpendicular means unrelated depends on the embedding.

Used in: ,

Source: ;

Denoiser

The network a trains and runs at every step: given a and how noisy it is, it predicts the noise (or the clean data), so a little can be taken away. It is usually a U-Net or a Transformer.

Used in: , ,

Source:

Dilation

Spacing out the inputs a reads, skipping some between each.

Doubling the spacing at each lets the reach grow exponentially with depth, so a few layers can see thousands of steps back.

Used in:

Source: ; Yu & Koltun 2015 (opens in a new tab)

Edge

A connection between two of a .

In a graph network the edges are the input's relations, such as bonds between atoms; in KAN each edge carries its own learned function instead of a single .

Used in: ,

Source: ;

Encoder and decoder

An encoder turns an input into an internal representation; a decoder turns a representation into an output.

Autoencoders, models, and U-Nets pair the two; BERT is an encoder alone and GPT a decoder alone.

Used in: , , , , , , , , , , ,

Source: ;

Energy

A single number a Hopfield network or Boltzmann machine gives each of its units, low for the states it has learned to favor.

In a Hopfield network no update can raise it, so the state settles into a minimum, often a stored pattern. A Boltzmann machine's random units keep changing, sometimes uphill; what settles is how often each state turns up, the low-energy ones most.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: ;

Equilibrium

For a network of random units, such as a Boltzmann machine, the point after enough updates where how often each turns up stops changing: low-energy states turn up most, though the units themselves keep changing. Boltzmann machines learn by comparing equilibrium with the data and with it free.

Used in: , ,

Source:

Feed-forward layer

The small MLP in each Transformer , applied to every position on its own after : it widens each , applies an , and narrows it back. It holds most of each block's , and a replaces it with many.

Used in: , , , , , , , ,

Source:

Filter

One learned pattern detector in a : a small grid of that, at each position, writes how strongly its pattern appears there.

A runs many filters, each making its own ; also called a .

Used in: , , ,

Source:

Gate

A learned multiplier, computed by the network and usually between 0 and 1, that scales a signal: near 0 shuts it out, near 1 lets it through.

LSTMs and GRUs compute their gates from the input and the previous , to decide what their state keeps, forgets, and shows. Mamba's selective state gates in a similar way, but from the input alone, which lets it train . xLSTM's exponential gates can go above 1. The guide draws a gate as a dotted line ending at a dot on the arrow it acts on.

Used in: , , , , ,

Source:

Gaussian bump

A bell-shaped response: largest at a center point and falling off smoothly with distance from it.

Each unit of a Gaussian radial basis network, the most common kind, responds this way to inputs near its center.

Used in:

Source:

Graph

A set of joined by , such as atoms and bonds, people and friendships, or roads and junctions. A graph network works on it directly, so it handles any number of nodes in any arrangement.

Used in:

Source:

Head

A small output on a shared network, turning its into one answer: a , the of each , a value. In , a head is one of several attention steps run side by side, each with its own , keys, and values, so each can look for something different.

Used in: , , , , , ,

Source:

Invertible

Able to be run backward exactly: every output comes from one input, which can be recovered. A is built from invertible chosen so that their effect on is cheap to compute. Most are coupling layers, which leave half the numbers as they are and use them to shift and scale the other half, so each layer is easy to undo.

Used in:

Source:

Kernel

A function scoring how alike two inputs are, such as a of the distance between them. Kernel methods such as support machines work entirely through such scores; each unit of a radial basis network is one kernel, measured against its center. (A 's is also called its kernel.)

Used in: ,

Source: ; Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab)

Latent

Hidden: describing what a model works with but never observes directly.

A latent space is where such live; a VAE or GAN draws a point there and decodes it into something new, and nearby points decode to similar things. An autoencoder's code is a latent .

Used in: , , , ,

Source:

Masking

Hiding part of what a network may see: swapped for a mask token for it to fill in (BERT, masked LLMs), or positions may not read (a ).

Used in: , ,

Source: ;

Message passing

How a network updates each : every neighbor sends it a message computed from its own , and the node combines them with its state. Repeating it lets information travel one farther each round.

Used in:

Source: ;

Mixture of experts

A made of many expert networks whose outputs a network, the , combines.

The original of 1991 weighted every expert; a mixture of experts, the usual kind today, picks only a few for each , so the model holds far more than any one token runs through. It can grow without costing proportionally more compute per token, though every expert must still be held in memory, and many of today's largest use it. The Routing entry steps through it.

Used in:

Source: Jacobs et al. 1991 (opens in a new tab);

Node

A point in a , such as an atom or a person, joined to others by .

In a graph network each node holds a , updated from its neighbors' ; in KAN a node just adds up what its edges bring.

Used in: ,

Source:

Normalization

Rescaling a 's numbers to a standard spread, so signals stay in a steady range as they pass through many layers and training stays stable.

Layer normalization works on each 's , batch normalization on each across a batch.

Used in: Most deep networks since 2015, and nearly every Transformer block.

Source: Ioffe & Szegedy 2015 (opens in a new tab); Ba, Kiros & Hinton 2016 (opens in a new tab)

Pooling

Shrinking a by summarizing each small , usually by its largest value.

It keeps whether a pattern appeared while forgetting exactly where, and lets later see more of the input for the same cost.

Used in:

Source: ; Riesenhuber & Poggio 1999 (opens in a new tab)

Position

A slot in a sequence or grid: one , one time step, one , or one place in a . on its own ignores order, so Transformers add positional encodings: the original added a fixed pattern of waves to each token's , BERT and ViT learn one per position, and most recent rotate and keys by their position instead (RoPE).

Used in: , , , , , , , , ,

Source: ; Su et al. 2021 (opens in a new tab)

Prior

The a draws its or from before generating, usually a plain . A VAE is trained to keep its codes close to it, so codes drawn from the prior usually decode to something plausible; where the codes of real data leave parts of the prior unfilled, from there can come out poorly.

Used in: , , ,

Source:

Query, key, and value

The three makes from each position, each by its own learned .

A position's query is compared with every key; the better the match, the more of that position's value it takes, like a lookup that returns a blend instead of one entry.

Used in: , , , , , , , ,

Source:

Read and write heads

The parts of a memory-augmented network that read from and write to its memory. Each produces soft over the memory's rows, by content or by location, so reading and writing are differentiable and can be trained by .

Used in:

Source:

Recurrence

Running the same network once per step of a sequence, passing a from each step to the next: a running summary of everything so far.

The state is what lets the network remember, and squeezing all of history into it is what makes long memories hard.

Used in: , , , , , , , ,

Source: ;

Reparameterization trick

Writing a random as the network's outputs plus independent , a mean plus a spread times a standard random number, so the error can be passed back through the sampling step. It is what lets a VAE train by .

Used in:

Source:

Residual connection

A path that carries a 's input around it and adds it to the layer's output, so the layer only has to learn a change.

It lets very train, because the signal, and in training its , can pass straight through. Also called a skip connection; U-Net's skip connections copy instead of adding.

Used in: , , , , , , , , , , ,

Source:

Residual stream

The running that carry through a : each reads it and adds its own output back, so the stream builds up every block's contribution.

Used in: , , , , , , , , , ,

Source: ;

Routing

Deciding where each input goes, or how much of it goes where.

A ' router scores the experts for each and sends it to only the top few, a selection; CapsNet's routing by agreement instead splits each 's output among all the higher capsules, by that favor those whose predictions agree with it.

Used in: ,

Source: ;

Solver

A numerical method that follows a forward in small steps, as for an ordinary differential equation (ODE). Flow-matching models this way, and so can (DDIM); diffusion's original sampler instead adds fresh at each step, a random version of the same walk. Better solvers take bigger steps with little in quality.

Used in: ,

Source: ;

Spline

A smooth curve made of short polynomial pieces joined end to end, shaped by a few control values.

The original KAN learns one spline per ; later versions swap in other curves that run faster.

Used in:

Source:

State

What a network carries from one step to the next: an RNN's , an LSTM's cell state beside it, or the matrix-valued state of linear and , which stays the same size however long the sequence grows. In the state is instead the situation the is in, which the sees.

Used in: , , , , , , , , , ,

Source: ; ; Sutton & Barto 2018 (opens in a new tab)

State space model

A built from linear updates of a hidden , an idea from control theory. Because each update is linear, training can compute a whole sequence , while generating runs one step at a time with a state of fixed size. Mamba makes the updates depend on the input (selective), so it can choose what to keep.

Used in: ,

Source: Gu, Goel & Ré 2021 (opens in a new tab);

Update rule

How a model writes each into its fixed-size , the main way such models differ. Plain linear accumulates: each token adds its , and nothing is ever removed, so old entries blur together as the state fills. Decay, as in RetNet and Mamba, shrinks the old state a little before each write, at a fixed rate or as the input decides, so the model can forget. The delta rule, as in DeltaNet, first reads what the state already returns for the key and writes only the difference from the new value, so it overwrites an entry rather than piling on top of it; Gated DeltaNet adds decay as well, so it can both forget and correct.

Used in: , ,

Source: ; Schlag, Irie & Schmidhuber 2021 (opens in a new tab);

Velocity

The direction and speed a point should move at a given moment, as a . Flow matching trains its network to output it, and follows it step by step; the guide marks it with an arrow.

Used in:

Source:

Window

The few neighboring positions an operation reads at once, such as a 's three inputs.

Sliding it along the input applies the same operation everywhere. Dilating it, skipping inputs between its reads, reaches farther with no extra ; widening it reaches farther too, but adds a weight for every input it gains.

Used in: , , ,

Source:

Objectives

Adversarial training

Training two networks as opponents, each improving by beating the other. In a GAN the gains when the mistakes its fakes for real data, and the discriminator when it doesn't; the contest pushes the fakes toward the real thing, though it can be unstable to train.

Used in:

Source:

Competitive learning

Units compete for each input: the one whose match it best wins and moves its weights toward it, and in a Kohonen map so do its neighbors on the map. Over many inputs each unit comes to stand for one kind of input.

Used in:

Source: ; Rumelhart & Zipser 1985 (opens in a new tab)

Contrastive learning

Training by pulling matching pairs together and pushing mismatched ones apart, such as a photo and its caption against the other captions in the batch.

Used in: ,

Source: ;

Hebbian learning

Strengthening the between two units that are active together, often summed up as cells that fire together wire together. A Hopfield network stores its patterns this way, in one pass, with no error passed back.

Used in:

Source: Hebb 1949 (opens in a new tab);

Likelihood

How probable a model finds some data (for continuous data such as images, a density). Training to raise it, usually its logarithm, teaches the model to assign high probability to real examples; a computes it exactly, a VAE a lower bound on its logarithm.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab);

Masked-token prediction

Training a model to fill in hidden from it, using the tokens on both sides.

BERT picks 15% of positions to predict and replaces most of them with a token (a few with a random token, a few left as they are). It suits a model that reads the whole text at once; a masked LLM by repeating it, unmasking a few tokens at a time.

Used in: ,

Source:

Next-token prediction

Training a model to predict each from the ones before it, so ordinary text supplies its own answers, and every position of a sequence is a training example at once.

It is how GPT-style learn.

Used in: , , , , , , , , , ,

Source: Bengio et al. 2003 (opens in a new tab);

Noise and denoising

Noise is random variation, here added on purpose. A denoising model learns to remove it, which teaches it what clean data looks like; repeats this a little at a time to , and a GAN's turns noise into data in one pass.

Used in: , , , , ,

Source: ;

Reconstruction

Training a network to reproduce its own input, usually through a narrow middle, so it must learn what matters about the data to get it back.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: ; Hinton & Salakhutdinov 2006 (opens in a new tab)

Variational bound

A lower bound on the logarithm of how probable a model with a hidden finds the data, trained in place of that , which can't be computed exactly; raising the bound usually raises the log-likelihood too, but not always: part of any gain can come from the bound growing tighter instead. A VAE's bound rewards rebuilding the input while keeping its codes close to its . train on a simplified form of the same bound.

Used in: ,

Source:

Training

Backpropagation

How a network finds which way to change each .

It passes the error back from the output, by layer, giving each weight its share of the blame, its gradient; gradient descent then moves every weight a small step the other way. Repeated over many examples, this is what training means for most networks here.

Used in: Nearly every network here; not the Hopfield network, the Boltzmann machines, or the Kohonen map, which learn by local rules.

Source:

Contrastive divergence

A fast way to train an RBM: start at the data, run only a step or a few, and nudge the toward the data and away from the short run's result. It approximates maximum-likelihood training without waiting for . Not related to contrastive learning.

Used in: ,

Source:

Distillation

Training a model, the student, to reproduce another's outputs, the teacher's: to make a smaller or faster copy. For and flow models it cuts from many steps to a few.

Used in: ,

Source: Hinton, Vinyals & Dean 2015 (opens in a new tab)

Fine-tuning

Training a model a little further, on a smaller dataset for a specific task, starting from its learned rather than from scratch. It is far cheaper than pretraining and adapts the model's to the task.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: ;

Gibbs sampling

from a network of random units by updating some of them, each drawn given the rest, over and over. Run long enough it reaches ; in an RBM a whole can be drawn at once, since its units don't connect to each other.

Used in: , ,

Source: Geman & Geman 1984 (opens in a new tab);

Loss

A number that measures how far a network's output is from what it should be; training lowers it.

Each panel's objective says what its loss rewards.

Used in: Nearly every network here; not the Hopfield network or the Kohonen map, which follow update rules instead.

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab)

Overfitting

Fitting the training examples so closely, quirks and errors included, that a network does worse on new data.

It shows when the on held-out examples, kept out of training, starts rising while the training loss still falls. Stopping there, early stopping, guards against it, as do and more data.

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab)

Post-training

Training a model further after , to shape how it behaves: on examples of good answers (instruction tuning), directly on people's preferences (as DPO does), or by such as RLHF, often several in turn. It turns a text predictor into an assistant.

Used in: ,

Source:

Pre-training

Training a model first on a large, general task, such as predicting words across much of the web, so it learns broadly useful before any specific use. A DBN pretrains one at a time; BERT and GPT pretrain on text.

Used in: , , , ,

Source: ;

Regularization

Anything that limits how freely a network fits its training data, so that it does better on new data. Weight decay pulls every weight a little toward zero; dropout switches off random units at each training step, so no unit can count on another; data augmentation shows each example in many variations, such as an image flipped or cropped; early stopping ends training once the stops falling. Some panels build it into their objective: the autoencoder's sparsity penalty, the autoencoder's noise, and the VAE's pull toward its .

Used in: , ,

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab); Srivastava et al. 2014 (opens in a new tab)

Sampling

Drawing an output at random from a model's instead of always taking the likeliest one, which is how give varied results.

Used in: , , , , , , , , , , ,

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab)

Self-supervised learning

Training on answers the data supplies itself: hide part of the input, or the next word, and ask the network for it. It needs no labels, so it can learn from vast amounts of text and images; it is the usual way to .

Used in: , , , , , ,

Source: ;

Supervised learning

Training on inputs paired with , the answers the network should give: labels people provided, such as what a photo shows, or targets from measurements, simulations, or a program, such as the copied sequences a Neural Turing machine learns to reproduce. The network is corrected toward each target. Most here, from the perceptron to ResNet, learn this way.

Used in: , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ,

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab)

Training and inference

Training adjusts a model's from data; inference runs the model on new inputs with its weights fixed. A model may be trained in several stages, retrained later, or updated as new data arrives, and each stage is costly; inference runs every time the model is used, so its cost per input matters most once a model is in use.

Used in: Every network here.

Source: Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab)

Unsupervised learning

Training with no answers at all: the network finds structure in the data on its own, such as , compact , or the data's overall shape. The Kohonen map, Boltzmann machines, and autoencoders learn this way.

Used in: , , , , , , , , ,

Source: ; Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville 2016 (opens in a new tab)

Vanishing gradient

The error passed back through many , or many steps of a , shrinking a little at each until the earliest barely learn.

It long made deep and recurrent networks hard to train; LSTM , , , and careful starting weights all answer it.

Discussed in: ,

Source: Hochreiter 1991 (opens in a new tab); Bengio, Simard & Frasconi 1994 (opens in a new tab)

Reinforcement learning

Action

What an agent does at each step, chosen by its : push left or right, move a piece, write a . The responds with a new and a .

Used in:

Source: Sutton & Barto 2018 (opens in a new tab)

Actor and critic

The two parts of an actor-critic method. The actor is the , choosing ; the critic estimates the value of a , the total still expected from it (the return), or of taking a given action in it. Comparing what happened with the critic's estimate tells the actor which actions did better than expected. The two can share one network or be separate ones.

Used in:

Source: ; Sutton & Barto 2018 (opens in a new tab)

Clipping

PPO's way of keeping each update small: it clips its objective, so once an 's has moved more than about 20% from before the update, in the direction that helps, pushing it further gains nothing. That removes the incentive for larger changes rather than strictly capping them, and keeps learning steady when one batch is lucky or unlucky.

Used in:

Source:

Environment

Everything outside the network that it acts on: a game, a simulator, a robot's surroundings, a person rating answers. It takes each and returns the next and a . The guide draws it as an outlined box.

Used in:

Source: Sutton & Barto 2018 (opens in a new tab)

Policy

In , the network that chooses : given the current , it usually gives the of each action, and one is drawn; a deterministic policy picks one directly. Policy-gradient methods train it directly, making well-rewarded actions more likely.

Used in:

Source: Sutton & Barto 2018 (opens in a new tab);

Reinforcement learning

Learning by trial and error. A network, the , chooses , and the returns : scores for how well things went. Training makes actions that led to more reward more likely. RLHF this way, with rewards from a model trained on people's preferences.

Used in:

Source: Sutton & Barto 2018 (opens in a new tab);

Reward

The score the returns after an , such as +1 for each step the pole stays up. Training aims for the most reward over time, not at each step.

Used in:

Source: Sutton & Barto 2018 (opens in a new tab);

Model families

Autoregressive model

A model that one piece at a time, each predicted from everything before it, feeding each output back in as the next input. Most work this way; language models fill in many at once instead.

Examples: , , , , ,

Source: ;

Diffusion

Generating data by learning to undo a gradual noising: a network is trained to remove a little at a time, then run from pure noise, step by step, to make something new. The Diffusion model panel draws it; diffusion LLMs do the same with .

Examples: ,

Source: ;

Generative model

A model that learns what its training data looks like well enough to make new examples of it: images, audio, or text. Some make a all at once (a GAN, a VAE's ), some refine step by step (, flow matching), and some write one piece at a time ( such as WaveNet and GPT).

Examples: , , , , , , , , , ,

Source: ;

Generator and discriminator

The two networks of a GAN. The generator turns random into a ; the discriminator sees real data and the generator's samples and guesses which is which. After training, only the generator is kept.

Used in:

Source:

Language model

A model of text: given some , it gives a for each token that could fit, usually the next one (), sometimes ones in between. Trained on vast amounts of text and then , large ones are today's chat assistants.

Examples: , , , , , , ,

Source: Bengio et al. 2003 (opens in a new tab);

Normalizing flow

A built from steps that turn simple into data and back, so it can compute its of any data exactly (a density). Flow matching trains a continuous one, whose steps are tiny moves along a learned ; its likelihood takes an solve to compute.

Examples: ,

Source: ;

Word2vec

A shallow network that learns a for every word from the words around it.

In its usual form, skip-gram with negative , each word's vector is trained to score the words really near it high and a few words drawn at random low. Words used in similar end up with similar vectors, so that king − man + woman lands near queen. GloVe and fastText are close relatives, and every since begins by looking up a learned for each .

Discussed in:

Source: Mikolov et al. 2013a (opens in a new tab); Mikolov et al. 2013b (opens in a new tab)

Tasks and data

Clustering

Grouping data points that lie close together, with no labels.

A radial basis network often places its centers by clustering the training data, and a Kohonen map clusters as it learns.

Used in: ,

Source: ;

Principal component

A direction along which data varies most; the first few give the best straight-line compression of the data.

A linear autoencoder with a narrow middle learns the same subspace, so it takes nonlinear to do better.

Discussed in:

Source:

Quantization

Rounding values to one of a fixed set of levels.

WaveNet quantizes each audio sample to one of 256 values, so it can predict the next as a choice among them with a . (Quantizing a model's to fewer bits, to save memory, is the same idea.)

Used in:

Source:

Segmentation

Labeling every pixel of an image with what it shows, such as cell or background, rather than labeling the image as a whole. A U-Net outputs a full-size map for it.

Used in:

Source:

Sequence to sequence

Mapping one sequence to another of possibly different length, such as a sentence to its translation: an reads the whole input, and a writes the output, usually one at a time. Translation drove the move from encoder–decoders to , and then to the Transformer.

Examples: ,

Source: Sutskever, Vinyals & Le 2014 (opens in a new tab); ;

Zero-shot

Doing a task with no training examples for that task. CLIP classifies an image by comparing it with captions such as “a photo of a dog”, so it can use labels from no training set, though its on web images and captions has likely seen similar images and words.

Used in:

Source:

Scale

Context window

How many a model can take into account at once: its working memory.

's cost grows with it, which is why and hybrid models aim at long contexts.

Discussed in: ,

Source:

KV cache

The a Transformer keeps for every earlier as it , so each new token can attend to them without recomputing them. It grows with the , and so does the cost of each new token; and keep a fixed-size instead.

Used in: , ,

Source: ; Pope et al. 2022 (opens in a new tab)

Parallelism

Working on every position of a sequence at once instead of one after another, which is what makes training on modern hardware fast. A Transformer trains on a whole sequence in one pass, while an RNN goes step by step, each waiting for the last; linear and are built so their can be computed in parallel too. carry it into , filling in many per pass.

Discussed in: , ,

Source: ;

Quadratic and linear time

Full compares every pair of positions, so its pairwise work grows with the square of the length: twice the text, four times that work.

The rest of the model grows only in step with the length, so for short texts the quadratic part need not dominate. and carry a fixed-size instead, so their work grows only in step with the length, but must squeeze all of the past into that state. Hybrids keep a few attention for direct access to earlier : still quadratic, but with far less quadratic work.
